title: New Frontiers
summary: Scientists are still inventing new vaccines today. They have made the first vaccines against a cancer-causing virus, against Ebola and against the malaria parasite, and they are working on flu, tuberculosis and the next pandemic.

sections.heading: A Toolbox That Keeps Growing
paragraphs: By the end of 2020, the world had watched scientists design, test and roll out brand-new COVID-19 vaccines in less than a year. It would be easy to think the story of vaccines ends there, with a happy finish line. It does not. Some of the most exciting vaccine work of the last twenty years has nothing to do with COVID-19 at all, and much of it is still going on as you read this.

One important thing to remember as you read: some of what follows is finished and approved, and some of it is research. Research means scientists are testing ideas. Many promising ideas fail in trials; that is how science sorts good ideas from bad ones. When something is still being tested, this chapter will say so clearly. And as always, this is a story about science and history. Questions about anyone's own health belong with a doctor and trusted adults.

sections.heading: An Empty Shell That Fights Cancer: HPV
paragraphs: Most people think of cancer as something that just happens inside the body, with no germ involved. That is usually true. But scientists have discovered that a few viruses can, over many years, push the cells they infect toward becoming cancer. One of the most important is the human papillomavirus, or HPV. There are more than a hundred types of HPV. Most cause no trouble at all, and the body clears them on its own. But a handful of 'high-risk' types, especially types 16 and 18, can stay hidden in cells for years and slowly cause changes that may become cancer of the cervix (the lower part of the womb), as well as some cancers of the throat, mouth and other parts of the body.

Stopping HPV infections could prevent a whole group of cancers decades later. But HPV is very hard to grow in a laboratory, so the old recipe of weakening or killing the whole germ could not work. The solution came from Ian Frazer, an immunologist born in Glasgow, Scotland, in 1953, who moved to Australia around 1981 and later worked at the University of Queensland in Brisbane, and from Jian Zhou, a talented virologist from China who joined him. Starting in 1990, they tried a clever trick. Instead of using the whole virus, they took the gene for L1, the main protein in the virus's outer coat. They put that gene into cells in the lab so the cells would make L1 protein. Then came the surprise: the L1 proteins clicked together all by themselves into round, hollow balls that looked almost exactly like real HPV particles under an electron microscope.

In March 1991 Zhou's wife, Xiao-Yi Sun, who was also a researcher, assembled these particles in the lab following Zhou's design. Scientists call them virus-like particles, or VLPs. Think of a VLP as a perfect toy model of a virus: it has the same outside shape, so the immune system learns to recognise it, but it is completely empty inside. It contains no genetic material, so it cannot infect anyone or copy itself. To the immune system, though, it looks like the real thing, and it makes lots of antibodies against it.

It took many more years, and the work of large companies, to turn this idea into real vaccines and test them in tens of thousands of volunteers. In 2006 the US Food and Drug Administration approved the first HPV vaccine, called Gardasil, made by Merck. Canada and Australia approved it the same year, and Frazer, who was named Australian of the Year in 2006, gave the first official HPV vaccinations in Australia. A second vaccine, Cervarix, made by GlaxoSmithKline, targets types 16 and 18. A newer version, Gardasil 9, covers nine HPV types.

Sadly, Jian Zhou did not live to see this. He died in 1999, still in his early forties, years before the vaccine he helped invent was approved. Today many scientists make a point of naming him, and Xiao-Yi Sun, whenever the HPV story is told.

The HPV vaccine is special for another reason too. It was one of the first vaccines made mainly to prevent cancer. (You met the other big one in part 16: the hepatitis B vaccine, which helps prevent liver cancer.) Because HPV cancers usually take decades to develop, the full effect is still arriving. But studies in countries that started vaccinating early, such as Scotland, Sweden and England, have already reported large drops in cervix cancer and pre-cancer among young women who were vaccinated as girls. The World Health Organization (WHO) now has a plan to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health problem, and one of its main targets is that 90% of girls should be fully vaccinated against HPV by age 15. In 2022, after studies showed that a single dose gave strong protection, WHO said a one-dose schedule could be used for younger people, which makes it much cheaper and easier for poorer countries to reach everyone.

sections.heading: Chasing Ebola Ring by Ring
paragraphs: Ebola is a virus disease first identified in 1976, near the Ebola River in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It spreads through direct contact with the body fluids of someone who is sick, or who has died of the disease. It causes high fever and severe illness, and in many outbreaks around half of the people infected have died.

Then, in December 2013, an outbreak began in Guinea and spread into Sierra Leone and Liberia. By the time it ended in 2016, it had become by far the largest Ebola epidemic ever recorded, with about 28,600 cases and about 11,300 deaths. Health workers, many of them local nurses and doctors, risked their lives caring for patients. Suddenly the whole world wanted an Ebola vaccine, fast.

Luckily, one was already waiting on a shelf. Years earlier, scientists at Canada's National Microbiology Laboratory in Winnipeg, part of the Public Health Agency of Canada, had built an experimental vaccine called rVSV-ZEBOV. It is a viral vector vaccine, a type you met briefly in part 12. The scientists took a mild animal virus called vesicular stomatitis virus, or VSV, which rarely bothers people, and swapped one of its genes for the gene of the Ebola virus's surface protein, called the glycoprotein. The result is a harmless 'disguised' virus wearing an Ebola costume. When it is injected, it copies itself a little and shows the immune system the Ebola glycoprotein, so the body learns to make antibodies against the real thing. It had protected monkeys in experiments, but it had never been tested in a big outbreak.

How do you run a fair test during an emergency, when cases are scattered and nobody knows where the next one will pop up? The answer was an old idea from smallpox days: ring vaccination, the strategy William Foege used in Nigeria (part 15). The trial, nicknamed 'Ebola ça Suffit!' ('Ebola, that's enough!'), began in Guinea in 2015. It was led by WHO with Guinea's health ministry and partners including Médecins Sans Frontières and Norwegian public health experts. Each time a new Ebola case was found, teams listed that person's contacts, and the contacts of those contacts. That group was called a ring.

At first, the rings were randomly split into two groups. Some rings were vaccinated straight away. Others were vaccinated 21 days later. Everyone got the vaccine in the end, but the delay let scientists compare the two groups. The early results, announced at the end of July 2015, were striking: among people vaccinated immediately, no Ebola cases appeared from ten days after vaccination onwards, while cases did still appear in the delayed group. Because the vaccine seemed so effective, the delayed group was dropped and everyone in the rings was offered the vaccine at once. Final results were published in the medical journal The Lancet at the end of 2016.

Some scientists pointed out that the trial had no placebo group and was fairly small, so claims of '100% protection' were too strong. That kind of careful criticism is normal in good science. Later experience gave a clearer answer: in Ebola outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of the Congo between 2018 and 2020, more than 90,000 people were vaccinated during one long outbreak in the Kivu region alone, and early estimates suggested very high protection.

In November 2019 the vaccine, now made by Merck and named Ervebo, received approval in Europe, and WHO prequalified it (approved it for purchase by UN agencies) within days. The US approved it in December 2019. Ervebo has one awkward feature: it must be stored frozen at very low temperatures, far colder than a home freezer, which makes it tricky to carry into hot, remote areas. Today an emergency stockpile of Ebola vaccine is kept ready, so that when a new outbreak starts, rings of people can be vaccinated within days instead of years.

sections.heading: Beating a Parasite: The First Malaria Vaccines
paragraphs: Every vaccine you have met so far in this story protects against a virus or a bacterium. Malaria is different. It is caused by a parasite, a single-celled living thing called Plasmodium, which is far bigger and more complicated than any virus. Five kinds infect people, and the deadliest, Plasmodium falciparum, is most common in Africa. The parasite is spread by the bites of certain female Anopheles mosquitoes. It does not pass directly from one person to another.

Malaria is one of the oldest and biggest killers of humankind. WHO estimates that in 2024 there were about 282 million malaria cases and about 610,000 deaths. About 95% of those deaths were in Africa, and about three out of every four deaths in the African region were children under five years old. Bed nets, insect sprays and medicines have saved millions of lives, but scientists dreamed for more than a century of adding a vaccine to that toolkit.

Why was it so hard? Imagine trying to make a 'wanted poster' for a criminal who keeps changing disguises. After a mosquito bite, the parasite travels in a form called a sporozoite to the liver. There it hides and multiplies inside liver cells for about a week. Then it bursts out in a new form that invades red blood cells, and later some parasites turn into yet another form that mosquitoes can pick up. Each stage wears different proteins on its surface. The parasite also has thousands of genes, compared with about a dozen for a virus like measles, and natural infection does not give people strong, lasting protection the way measles or smallpox did.

The first breakthrough began in the late 1980s at a company laboratory in Belgium, then called SmithKline Beecham Biologicals and today part of GSK, working with the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research in the United States. Their vaccine, called RTS,S (brand name Mosquirix), aims at the very first stage, the sporozoite, to stop the parasite before it can settle in the liver. It joins part of the parasite's main surface protein, the circumsporozoite protein, to the hepatitis B surface antigen, the same protein used in the hepatitis B vaccine you met in part 16. Together they assemble into virus-like particles, a bit like the HPV vaccine. A strong adjuvant called AS01 helps the immune system respond. (The odd name RTS,S comes from the bits of protein it contains: R for a 'repeat' region, T for a T-cell target region, and S for the hepatitis B surface antigen.)

Making it work took about three decades of trials, with support from the charity PATH and the Gates Foundation. A large Phase 3 trial in seven African countries found that the vaccine roughly halved malaria cases in young children over the first year, though protection faded over time and a fourth dose helped. That is far from perfect, but in places where a child might catch malaria several times a year, even partial protection can prevent a huge number of illnesses.

In 2019, Malawi, Ghana and Kenya began a big pilot programme, giving the vaccine to young children through ordinary clinics. Researchers watched closely for safety and for real-world benefits. The results showed fewer hospital admissions for severe malaria, and the vaccine was given safely to well over a million children. In October 2021, WHO recommended RTS,S for wide use in children living where malaria is common. It was the first vaccine ever recommended against a human parasitic disease, a true milestone in medical history.

Just two years later a second vaccine arrived. R21/Matrix-M was developed by the Jenner Institute at the University of Oxford (named, of course, after Edward Jenner) with partners including the Kenya Medical Research Institute, and it is manufactured by the Serum Institute of India, one of the world's biggest vaccine makers. It uses a similar idea to RTS,S, with a different adjuvant called Matrix-M. In trials it reached about 75% efficacy against malaria in young children in places where malaria comes in seasonal waves. Ghana became the first country to approve it, in April 2023, and WHO recommended it in October 2023. Because the Serum Institute can make huge numbers of doses, it plans to produce well over a hundred million doses a year. African countries began adding these vaccines to regular childhood schedules in 2024, alongside bed nets, medicines and mosquito control rather than instead of them.

sections.heading: Old Enemies, New Weapons: RSV and Tuberculosis
paragraphs: Respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, is a common virus that usually causes a cold. Almost every child catches it by the age of two. But in tiny babies and in older adults it can infect the lungs and cause serious breathing problems, and it sends many people to hospital each winter.

The search for an RSV vaccine has a sad history that taught scientists an important lesson. In the 1960s, researchers tested a vaccine made of RSV killed with a chemical called formalin. Instead of protecting children, it made some of them sicker when they later caught RSV naturally, and two children died. The immune system had been trained to make the wrong kind of response. That shock made scientists extremely careful, and for more than fifty years there was no RSV vaccine at all.

The key that finally unlocked the problem came from structural biology, the science of seeing the exact shapes of molecules. In 2013, Jason McLellan, Barney Graham and their colleagues at the US National Institutes of Health mapped the structure of RSV's fusion protein, called F, the protein the virus uses to break into cells. They found that F has two shapes: a 'before' shape (prefusion) and an 'after' shape (postfusion). The best protective antibodies attack the 'before' shape, but the protein naturally flips into its 'after' shape, a bit like a mousetrap snapping shut. The team found ways to lock it in the 'before' shape. You may recognise the names: the same scientists later used similar tricks to stabilise the coronavirus spike protein for COVID-19 vaccines (part 18).

This work paid off in 2023. In May 2023, the US approved Arexvy, made by GSK, for adults aged 60 and over, followed by Abrysvo, made by Pfizer. In August 2023 Abrysvo was also approved for use during pregnancy, so that a mother's antibodies pass to her baby and help protect the newborn during its first months. In 2024 an mRNA RSV vaccine, Moderna's mRESVIA, was approved too.

Tuberculosis, or TB, is an even older foe. You met its bacterium in part 7, when Robert Koch identified it in 1882, and the BCG vaccine in part 9, first given in 1921. Astonishingly, more than a hundred years later, BCG is still the only TB vaccine in common use. It helps protect babies and young children from the most severe forms of TB, but its protection for teenagers and adults, who spread most TB, varies enormously between studies, from very little to fairly good. Meanwhile TB still kills more than a million people a year, making it one of the deadliest infectious diseases on Earth.

Several new TB vaccines are now in large trials. One, called M72/AS01E, combines two TB proteins with the same kind of adjuvant used in the RTS,S malaria vaccine. In a trial in Kenya, South Africa and Zambia, adults who already carried TB bacteria without being ill were about half as likely to develop TB disease over three years if they had the vaccine. That was promising enough to launch a much larger Phase 3 trial in 2024 with many thousands of volunteers, which is expected to run until the end of the 2020s. Another candidate, MTBVAC, is a weakened form of the human TB bacterium itself and is also in Phase 3 trials. Nobody yet knows if these will succeed. If one does, it could be the first new TB vaccine in over a century.

sections.heading: Ideas Still in the Lab
paragraphs: Everything in this section is research, not a promise. First, the universal flu vaccine. In part 11 you learned that flu vaccines are updated every year because flu viruses keep changing. The flu virus is covered in a protein called hemagglutinin, which is shaped a little like a lollipop or a mushroom, with a round head on top of a stalk. Most of the antibodies our bodies make attack the head, but the head changes constantly, so last year's antibodies may not fit this year's virus. The stalk changes much less. Scientists at places such as the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York have designed vaccines that give people a series of 'mismatched' heads on the same stalk, hoping to steer the immune system toward the stalk instead. Early human trials have been encouraging, but at least one large trial of a 'universal' candidate found no protection at all. As of the mid-2020s, no universal flu vaccine has been approved.

Second, cancer vaccines. There are two very different ideas here. Preventive cancer vaccines, like the HPV and hepatitis B vaccines, stop cancer-causing viruses from infecting people. Therapeutic cancer vaccines are meant to help the immune system attack a cancer that is already there. That is much harder, because cancer cells come from the body's own cells, and the immune system is trained not to attack 'self'. Only a few therapeutic cancer vaccines have ever been approved, such as sipuleucel-T for advanced prostate cancer in 2010, and many others have failed in trials.

The newest approach is personalised. Cancer cells pile up mistakes in their DNA, and some of those mistakes create unusual proteins, called neoantigens, that healthy cells do not have. Researchers can read the genes of a patient's tumour, use computers to pick out the most promising neoantigens, and then build an mRNA vaccine carrying instructions for those exact targets, all within a matter of weeks. Each vaccine is made for just one person. Companies including Moderna with Merck, and BioNTech, the company you met in part 18, are testing this idea in trials for skin cancer (melanoma), pancreatic cancer and other cancers. Some mid-stage results have been encouraging, but large trials still need to show whether these vaccines really help, and for whom.

Third, vaccines without needles. Many people dislike injections, and needles need trained staff and safe disposal. A few vaccines can already be swallowed (like Sabin's polio drops) or sprayed into the nose (like one kind of flu vaccine). Researchers are also building microneedle patches: small sticky patches covered with hundreds of tiny points, each shorter than a millimetre, that carry the vaccine just into the top layers of the skin and then dissolve. Patches could be easier to transport, could perhaps be given without a fully trained nurse, and leave no sharp needles to throw away. Patches for measles and rubella have been tested in young children in early trials, but they are not yet in routine use.

Fourth, vaccines that do not need a fridge. Remember the cold chain from part 12: most vaccines must stay between 2°C and 8°C all the way from the factory to the clinic. In very hot places with unreliable electricity, that is one of the biggest obstacles to protecting children. Scientists are experimenting with dry powders, special sugars that 'freeze' proteins in place like insects in amber, and tougher vaccine designs. A vaccine that could sit happily in a backpack for weeks would be a gift to health workers everywhere.

sections.heading: Getting Ready for Disease X
paragraphs: What about the next pandemic? Nobody knows what germ will cause it, so WHO and scientists sometimes give it a placeholder name: Disease X. Preparing for Disease X means building tools in advance, so that the world can respond faster than it did in 2020.

One of the main groups doing this is CEPI, the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations. It was launched in January 2017 at the World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, Switzerland, by the governments of Norway and India, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, the Wellcome Trust and the World Economic Forum, and it is based in Oslo, Norway. CEPI was partly inspired by the lesson of Ebola: vaccine research for dangerous but rare diseases had been neglected until it was almost too late. CEPI funds work on vaccines for diseases such as Lassa fever, Nipah virus, MERS and Rift Valley fever, which have caused deadly outbreaks but have few or no approved vaccines.

In 2022 CEPI and its partners set a bold goal called the 100 Days Mission: to be able to produce a safe, effective vaccine against a new pandemic threat within 100 days of identifying it. To see how ambitious that is, count the days for COVID-19. The coronavirus's genetic sequence was shared on 11 January 2020, and the first vaccine was authorised in the UK on 2 December 2020. That is 326 days, which was a world record, yet the 100 Days Mission aims to cut it by more than two-thirds. To get there, scientists are building 'libraries' of vaccine designs for whole families of viruses, so that much of the work is already done before a new virus appears.

There is also unfinished business from earlier in this story: polio. In 1988, when the Global Polio Eradication Initiative began, wild polio paralysed an estimated 350,000 people a year in more than 125 countries. Since then cases have fallen by more than 99%. Two of the three types of wild poliovirus have been eradicated: type 2 was certified gone in 2015 and type 3 in 2019. India was certified polio-free as part of its region in 2014, and Africa was declared free of wild polio in 2020. As of the mid-2020s, wild poliovirus is still passed on in only two countries, Pakistan and Afghanistan. Polio is not eradicated yet, and stopping the last chains of infection in those areas, where conflict and difficult terrain make vaccination hard, is one of the toughest jobs in global health.

There is one more complication, which you met in part 14. In places where few children are vaccinated, the weakened virus in Sabin's oral vaccine can very rarely spread from child to child for a long time and change back into a form that can cause paralysis. Scientists call these outbreaks 'vaccine-derived' polio. They are rare, and they can be stopped by vaccinating more children. To reduce the risk, scientists have designed a new, more genetically stable oral vaccine called nOPV2, first used in 2021 under an emergency listing and given full WHO prequalification in December 2023. The long-term plan is to stop using live oral polio vaccine once wild polio is gone, so that only the inactivated vaccine that Jonas Salk pioneered remains.

Look at how many ideas from earlier chapters appear in these new frontiers: Foege's ring vaccination stopping Ebola, the hepatitis B antigen inside a malaria vaccine, Jenner's name on an Oxford institute, Sabin's and Salk's vaccines still fighting polio, and mRNA reaching toward cancer. New inventions almost never appear from nowhere. They are built on everything that came before. Which makes this the perfect moment to stop, turn around, and look back along the whole road, from a pinch of scab powder blown up a nose to a strand of genetic code in a tiny bubble of fat.

deepDive: Many of the new frontiers share one theme: vaccines are increasingly designed rather than discovered. Jenner and Pasteur worked with whole organisms they could not see; the HPV, RSV and malaria vaccines were built around single, carefully chosen proteins. Structure-based design, used for RSV's prefusion F protein, uses X-ray crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy to see an antigen at near-atomic detail, then adds small mutations, such as extra chemical bonds, that lock it into the shape that provokes the best antibodies. The RSV story also shows why history matters. The formalin-inactivated RSV vaccine of the 1960s caused 'enhanced respiratory disease', most likely because it presented the post-fusion form of F and steered the immune system toward antibodies that bound poorly and inflammatory responses that did harm. Regulators still examine new respiratory vaccines for this risk. Malaria shows the limits of the protein approach. RTS,S and R21 target only the sporozoite stage; a single sporozoite that escapes and reaches the liver can still start an infection, which helps explain why efficacy is partial and fades without boosters. Researchers are testing blood-stage and 'transmission-blocking' vaccines that would stop mosquitoes picking up the parasite, and combinations of stages. Debates also surround how trials are designed. The Guinea Ebola trial used 'cluster randomisation' (whole rings, not individuals, were randomised) with delayed vaccination rather than a placebo, because withholding a possibly life-saving vaccine during an epidemic seemed unethical. Critics, including a 2017 report from the US National Academies, argued its small number of cases made the precise efficacy figure uncertain, even though the vaccine was clearly protective. Finally, the 100 Days Mission depends as much on manufacturing, regulation and fairness as on science. During COVID-19, high-income countries received most early doses; many experts argue that building factories and regulatory capacity in Africa, Asia and Latin America, such as the planned R21 production in Ghana, is essential if the next fast vaccine is to reach everyone quickly.
funFact: The RTS,S malaria vaccine contains a piece of the hepatitis B virus's surface protein, so a vaccine invented to fight a liver-attacking virus ended up helping to carry the first-ever vaccine against a parasite.

check.q: What was special about the RTS,S vaccine that WHO recommended in October 2021?
check.a: It was the first vaccine recommended against a human parasite (malaria)
wrong: It was the first vaccine made with mRNA
It was the first vaccine against a cancer-causing virus
It was the first vaccine that needed no refrigeration
